docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
These docs contain hardware build instructions as well as a high-level overview of the software layout. For details on running the software for teleoperation, see the software repository.

Bill of Materials Parts list with pricing and vendor links. Assembly Build the backpack and leader arms. Software Install and configure the ModPack software stack.

docs.title: Assembly Overview
docs.text: ModPack consists of a core "backpack" interface that the rest of the modules such as the leader arms attach to. Pictured above are the two leader arm configurations currently supported by ModPack, as well as an exploded view of the backpack itself.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text:
• Backpack: Walks through 3D printing up to attaching mounted components and wiring the power circuit.
  • Arms: Details fabrication of both ARX and RB-Y1m leaders arms as well as integration into the backpack.

Tip

It is highly recommended that you start with the backpack, as testing the arms requires the power circuit.

docs.title: General Motor Setup
docs.text: Before assembling either arm variant, each Dynamixel servo must be configured with a unique ID and the correct baud rate. This is done using the Dynamixel Wizard 2.0.

docs.title: Installing Dynamixel Wizard 2.0
docs.text: Download and install Dynamixel Wizard 2.0 from the ROBOTIS website. Connect your U2D2 interface board to your computer via USB. Note that all motors except the XL-330 require 12 V power through the power circuit while the XL-330 requires installation of the 5 V stepdown converter before being plugged in.

docs.title: Preparing the XL-330 (5V Stepdown)
docs.text:
The XL-330 servo operates at 5V, while the rest of the motor chain runs at 12V. A 5V stepdown converter must be installed on the link before the holder (for both leader arm variants) in the chain before connecting it to power.

  1. Cut the end of the wire that will come out of the motor preceding the XL-330. Cut another Dynamixel connector in the same way, which will be used from the converter and signal line to the XL-330. You will need to cut through the signal line as well.
  2. Use the ENGINEER PA-09 crimper to attach JST crimps from the JST XH 2.54mm connector kit to the ground and power lines of the incoming motor \(V_{in}\). Slot them into the 2-pin female pin housing, connecting to VIN and GND on the converter.
  3. Wire the stepdown converter inline. 12V in from the upstream motor (XM430-W350 for ARX5, XM430-W210 for RB-Y1m), 5V out to the XL-330 power pin. Refer to the XL-330 e-manual for pinout details. Connect the signal line to one end of a WAGO connector.
  4. Use the pre-crimped cables with the 2-pin housing to connect to \(V_{out}\) and GND on the converter. On the other end of the cable, connect another 2-pin housing.
  5. Using the second Dynamixel connector that has the header cut off, use the ENGINEER PA-09 crimper to attach JST crimps from the JST XH 2.54mm connector kit to the ground and power lines of what will become the line to the XL-330 motor. Attach a 2-pin male header to the ground and power lines, connecting this to the female 2-pin out from the converter \(V_{out}\) and GND. Connect the remaining signal line to the other end of the WAGO connector.
  6. Mount the board on the last link before the holder (applies to either arm) with M2x6 screws and the M2 heat-set inserts.
Top view Bottom view Wiring

docs.title: Setting Motor IDs
docs.text:
Motors must be assigned unique IDs so the arm controller can address each joint individually. It is easiest to configure one motor at a time.

  1. Open Dynamixel Wizard 2.0 and click Scan to detect the connected motor.
  2. Select the motor from the device list.
  3. In the control table, find the ID field and set it to the desired joint number. Refer to the arm-specific section below for the correct ID assignment per joint.
  4. Click Save to write the value to the motor.
  5. Disconnect the motor and repeat for the next one.

docs.title: Setting Baud Rate
docs.text:
All motors must be set to the same baud rate used by the arm controller.

  1. With the motor connected and detected, find the Baud Rate field in the control table.
  2. Set the baud rate to 1000000 (1 Mbps).
  3. Click Save.

docs.title: Attaching Servo Horns
docs.text:
Before inserting motors into 3D-printed links, attach the servo horn to the motor output shaft.

  1. Align the servo horn with the spline on the output shaft. The horn is keyed so it will only fit in one orientation, so do not force it.
  2. Press the horn firmly onto the shaft until it is fully seated.
  3. Secure with the included horn screw.

docs.title: Backpack Build
docs.text:
In this section, we will walk through all of the necessary steps to fabricate and assemble the ModPack core.

Before You Begin

The U2D2 must be assembled onto the U2D2 Power Hub Board before installing it in the backpack.

docs.title: Tools Required
docs.text:
• Soldering iron with heat-set insert tip
  • Hex wrench set (2.5 mm, 3 mm, 5 mm)
  • Small crescent wrench

docs.title: 3D Prints
docs.text:
Tool Required

FDM 3D printer (Bambu Labs H2D or X1 Carbon recommended)

All backpack components were printed on a Bambu Labs H2D (large panels) or Bambu X1 Carbon (smaller pieces). The backpack is split into two halves so each half fits on a standard print bed.

docs.title: Heat Set Inserts
docs.text:
After printing, we install heat set inserts to provide rigid mounting points for bolts. We find a good temperature for the soldering iron is 220 C.

Tool Required

Soldering iron, optionally with a heat-set insert tip.

Heat set insert locations on the backpack panels.

Use the above diagram to find the heat set insert locations. Use the 94180A321 M2.5x3.4 heat-set inserts.

docs.title: Brackets
docs.text: Once heat sets are in, use the 97763A822 M5x16 button head screws to fasten the 3D printed brackets.

docs.title: Latches
docs.text:
Latch mounting hole locations.

Next, install the latches using 97763A822 M5x16 button head screws and 93625A200 M5 nylon lock nuts.

docs.title: Mounting Arm Bars
docs.text:
The two vertical 40x40 bars are the mounting points for the leader arms. The dotted lines indicate where to secure the bars using the sliding nuts and M5 bolts described in the callout below.

Mounting the arm bars

The leader arms mount to two vertical 40×40 T-slot extrusion bars that slot into the top of the front panel of the backpack. Once you have installed the bar brackets (x4) with the 91292A832 M2x8 socket head screws, slide the 40x40 bars into place, securing them by following the dotted callouts with 97763A822 M5x16 button head screws and the T-slot sliding T-nuts.

docs.title: Mounting Electronics
docs.text: Mounting points for electronics.

docs.title: U2D2 Power Hub and REV Mini PDP
docs.text:
Note the direction of the bolts for the REV as well as for the U2D2 offsets.

Use the provided screw offsets, securing the back of the U2D2 board with the 91292A016 M2.5x12 socket head screws and 93475A210 M2.5 washers.

With the bolt head (91290A252 M5x25 socket head screw) on the inside of the backpack, mount the REV Mini Power Module to the side of the backpack, securing with a 93625A200 M5 nylon lock nut.

docs.title: Shelves
docs.text:
Bottom shelf with two latches. Note that you can only install one on each side, though mounting points are provided for two on each side. It is up to you what configuration you want.

Install the shelves in bottom-up order, as the bottom shelf has a set of stands that cannot be fit in the backpack if the shelf above is installed. Pictured above is the bottom-most shelf along with the attached latches that hold the components in. Tighten such that you can still move the latches to slide components in and out.

docs.title: iPhone Mount
docs.text:
Attach the iPhone mount with zipties by looping the ties through the backpack, as shown below.

Side view and top view

docs.title: Backpack Straps
docs.text:
Upper straps: Loop a strap through the backpack, then assemble using the multi-purpose buckle set so that the buckle faces outwards.

For buckle assembly, see specific manufacturer instructions here.

Lower straps: Loop the harness strap directly through the backpack hole as shown below. More detailed installation steps can be found on the manufacturer's page. Adjust tightness as needed.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Cable Management

To reduce the amount of wire outside of the backpack, we recommend that excess wiring is routed through the backpack slots.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: There are three power banks that serve the backpack, one for each leader arm (if attached) and one for the mini PC. This section will walk through how to wire the associated power circuit, starting with preparing leader arm power and moving to the Mini PC. Note that the Vision Pro connects to its dedicated charger and is not part of the circuit.

docs.title: Power Banks → REV Mini Power Modules → U2D2 Power Hub Boards
docs.text:
Attach the USBC end of the PD Trigger Cable to OUT1 of the UGREEN 145W Power Banks. Next, insert the other end of the PD trigger cable to the Female DC Barrel Jack.

Next, split the remaining end of the pigtail barrel jack and lift up on the largest tabs on the REV MPM, inserting red wire into the red slot and black wire into the associated slot.

Before attaching the output cable to the REV MPM, first insert the 5 A fuse that comes with the kit into the slot you plan to use for the arms (you can choose any). Split the free end of the Male DC Barrel Jack, lifting the tabs of the associated channel where the fuse is and insert red to red, black to black. The U2D2 Power Hub Board will be what connects the leader arms to power and communication.

docs.title: Mini PC Power
docs.text: The remaining UGREEN 145W Power Bank uses the PC Cable to directly connect to the Mini PC. Again, use OUT1 for the USB C cable.

docs.title: Software Overview
docs.text:
ModPack software is built around three parts:

  1. Bridge — SDK library that robot controllers import to receive commands and publish state
  2. Modules — self-contained modpack-side processes (GELLO leader arms, logger, Vision Pro, base)
  3. Orchestration — lifecycle engine that starts/stops modules and manages episodes
flowchart LR
    subgraph ModpackSide["Modpack side"]
        Orchestration["Orchestration\n(coordinator, episode manager, registry)"]
        Modules["Modules\n(GELLO, logger, vision_pro, etc.)"]
        Orchestration -. starts/stops, gates activation .-> Modules
    end

    subgraph RobotSide["Robot side"]
        Runner[Robot runner] --> Bridge["Bridge\n(modpack/bridge.py)"]
    end

    RMQ(("Robot Message Queue (RMQ)"))

    Modules <-- commands / state --> RMQ
    RMQ <-- commands / state --> Bridge

The two sides communicate only through the RMQ bus, and topology is set per-robot in config.yaml.

Reference

The repository map, CLI flags, config schema, and control-key tables live in the code repo: README · robots/README · orchestration/README

  • Configuration — How to setup within ModPack repo
  • Modules — Vision Pro head tracking and iPhone base control

docs.title: ModPack Mini PC
docs.text:
Follow the TidyBot2 software setup guide and navigate to Mini PC Setup to configure the Mini PC, including OS installation and SSH.

Performance tuning

On the ModPack PC, limit the CPU frequency, per the CPU-frequency step in the ModPack README, so the logging load does not lag control.

docs.title: Network Setup
docs.text: The Mini PC and the robot PC must be on the same network. For best performance, connect the robot to a dedicated WiFi network rather than a shared one.

docs.title: ModPack Software
docs.text:
Clone the repo and create the conda environment:

conda env create -f environment.yaml
conda activate modpack

docs.title: Robot-specific setup
docs.text: Each robot needs additional setup not covered above (for example building arx5_interface or the rby1-sdk), documented in its README: arx5/README · rby1/README

docs.title: Entry Point
docs.text:
The main entry point(s) for launching teleoperation with ModPack are the following commands. 

# For ARX robot
python -m modpack --gello --robot arx5

# For RB-Y1m
python -m modpack --gello --robot rby1

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
There are two ways to structure the connection between the ModPack PC and the robot PC. The mode is set per-robot via topology in config.yaml — see robots/README.

Managed topology — The ModPack PC manages everything: it launches the robot PC's teleop on startup and kills it on shutdown.

  • You → ModPack PC → activates Robot PC teleop
  • On shutoff: ModPack kills Robot PC teleop automatically

docs.title: Example: ARX5
docs.text:
Launching the modpack command handles the lifecycle of both the ModPack PC and the robot PC automatically. To enable this, you must set up passwordless SSH from the ModPack PC to the robot PC. 

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

# Fill in with your user and hostname for robot PC
ssh-copy-id user@hostname

Unmanaged topology — You manage both PCs independently.

  • You → ModPack PC (separately) and You → Robot PC teleop (separately)
  • On shutoff: stop the robot command/teleop loop first, then stop the ModPack (recommended for safety)

docs.title: Example: RB-Y1m
docs.text:
For RB-Y1m, the order of operations is to first run the above modpack python command, activate relevant subsystems as will be discussed, and then run command below. 

# For RB-Y1m
python modpack/robots/rby1/scripts/rby1_wbc_teleop_gello.py

docs.title: CLI Flags
docs.text:
Reference

The full CLI flag list (--gello, --robot, --vp-stream-mode, --vp-bypass-neck, --modules, …) lives in the README.

docs.title: Episode and Activation Controls
docs.text: The keys s, v, and q control episode logging, module activation, and shutdown once the modpack command is launched.

docs.title: Episode Control (s key)
docs.text:
Reference

The tap-pattern table (start/stop/pause/resume/delete) lives in the README.

docs.title: Module Activations (v key)
docs.text: The specific number of taps of the v key required to activate each module (such as leader arms, vision pro, etc) is contained within the activation_buttons section of each robot's config.yaml, where the number next to each module name is the number of quick, consecutive taps required to activate.

docs.title: Shutdown (q key)
docs.text:
Pressing q at any point after launching the modpack command will shutdown ModPack code.

Warning

The code is not responsive to ctrl+c.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
ModPack uses two YAML config files: a global networking config (modpack_config.yaml) and a per-robot hardware and runtime config (robots/<name>/config.yaml).

Reference

The full key reference for both config files lives in the code repo: README · robots/README · orchestration/README

docs.title: modpack_config.yaml
docs.text: Lives at modpack/modules/modpack_config.yaml and controls RMQ server networking across all robots.

docs.title: modpack/robots/<name>/config.yaml
docs.text: Lives at modpack/robots/<name>/config.yaml. Controls all robot-specific hardware and runtime behavior.

docs.title: GELLO Hardware (gello key)
docs.text:
Reference

GELLO module internals (RMQ topics, lifecycle): gello/README.

docs.title: Port Configuration
docs.text: As indicated by the GELLO software readme, you can find the path to the U2D2 once you plug into the ModPack mini PC by using ls /dev/serial/by-id, where the device should be in the form usb-FTDI_USB__-__Serial_Converter. The baudrate parameter should match what you have set in the Dynxamixel Wizard 2.0

docs.title: Motor Configuration
docs.text:
Zero position offsets/robot joint signs and joint offsets/joint signs are all crucial for safe and correct control of any target robot. They serve two distinct purposes.

  • zero_position_offsets/robot_joint_signs: Accounts for the difference between URDF and arm zero position, enabling accurate gravity compensation. Unless you use different URDFs from those provided, this does not need to change.
  • joint_offsets/joint_signs: Accounts for difference between installed motor zero and robot zero positions and directionality of motors. Ideally these are zero, but are left in to account for any offset as to not make people re-install motors. These offsets need to be calibrated for each setup.

Warning

Do not run teleoperation without first calibrating the joint offsets. For joint signs, only change as needed.

To calibrate joint offsets for either arm, use the script zero_calib.py. This will also calibrate the gripper open and close angles, which are necessary to account for installation angle.

Reference

Usage and steps: scripts/calibration/README.

docs.title: Current Limits
docs.text: Per-motor current limits bound motor output to ensure safe gravity compensation and reasonable haptic feedback. Each arm motor has a current_limit (the overall ceiling), plus separate gravity_current_limit and contact_current_limit budgets for gravity compensation and haptic contact feedback; these are converted to torque internally using the motor's torque constant. The gripper, which is position-controlled, has only a current_limit. We have set up limits that are comfortable for general use, but users are free to tune these parameters within reason, noting the maximum current allowed per motor and the maximum total current the battery setup is able to provide.

docs.title: Control Parameters
docs.text: Control parameters such as kp and kd are set to reasonable values for gravity compensation, but users are free to tune.

Logging-stream config: modpack/modules/logger/README.

docs.title: Vision Pro
docs.text:
To use the Vision Pro, you will first need to install the Vision Pro app and connect to the same network as the ModPack PC as well as robot PC if applicable. After cloning the repo, refer to how to upload to the vision pro here. When ready to use, open the app and click the gear icon in the upper right corner of the app. From here, enter the ip of the computer used to launch the Vision Pro process.

Reference

Module internals, activation flow, and VP_BYPASS_NECK: vision_pro/README.

Note

You need Xcode to build the Vision Pro app, so the build machine must be a Mac.

docs.title: Neck Configuration (ARX Robot Only)
docs.text: If using the ARX5-based mobile robot described in Vision-in-Action, the specific CAN interface, control frequency, and iPhone camera configuration used are defined in neck_config.yaml within the arx5 robot folder. Refer to the Vision-in-Action hardware documentation for how to set up the CAN interface, and to its point-cloud streaming instructions for how to set up RGB/PCD streaming on the neck iPhone.

docs.title: Using the App
docs.text: When you open the app, you will see a screen that can be moved. Move the window up and above your head such that it is out of view, as the actual display will show up in front of you. When using the app to control the neck, be sure to be still and face forward until you see that the robot neck has started to move.

docs.title: Base Control with iPhone
docs.text:
To use the iPhone for base control, you must first download a compatible browser. From the advice of the tidybot++ documentation we use XR Browser, which can be found in the app store. Next, you must connect your phone to the same network as the ModPack PC as well as robot PC if applicable. Next, navigate to the ip address of the hosting computer (either ModPack or robot PC depending on layout) on port 5000. You will then want to mount the iPhone on the phone mount with the screen facing towards the operator's back as shown below.

iPhone mounted with screen facing towards the operator's back.

When using a robot that is not the tidybot base that controls its own base separately (such as the RB-Y1m), use the use_mock_base flag (under module_overrides.base) in the robot config.yaml. To activate the base, tap the appropriate activation keys as explained in Configuration. Currently, the base will only move once the s key is tapped, indicating the start of an episode.

Reference

Base module internals (RMQ topics, use_mock_base): base/README.
